# Power from Magneto (for LED)

Harvesting power directly from a magneto to run accessories like an LED headlight is a classic engineering trade-off between simplicity and reliability. You are correct that small two-stroke or single-cylinder engines, such as those found in hovercrafts and many snowblowers, lack a dedicated alternator. Instead, they rely on a permanent magnet rotor spinning past stationary coils to induce a high-voltage AC pulse for the ignition system. While this setup works perfectly for creating a spark via the points or electronic ignition module, it is not inherently designed for continuous power output.

### The Physics of Magneto Output

A magneto generates electricity only when the engine is running. It has no external electrical input and no battery backup. When you connect a load to the low-voltage coil, you are drawing current that was originally intended to charge an internal capacitor or feed the ignition coil. On high-speed applications like hovercrafts or snowblowers, the RPMs can be in the thousands. At these speeds, the magneto is capable of generating significant voltage spikesâoften exceeding 40V on the primary side due to transformer actionâbut the current availability remains low.

The critical constraint here is the engine's inertia. A magneto acts as a generator, but it also relies on the engine's rotational momentum to maintain speed. If you attach a load that draws too much current, the back-electromotive force (back-EMF) will increase, effectively creating a drag torque on the crankshaft. This manifests as a measurable drop in RPM or a rough idle. If your headlight driver requires more than the engine can supply without stalling, the system will fail immediately upon startup or when the load spikes during operation.

### Implementing the Connection Safely

Since your LED unit has an internal regulator and can tolerate up to 40V, the primary concern is not voltage tolerance but current stability and noise. The magneto output is AC, even if the ignition coil internally converts it for spark generation. Connecting a DC load directly across a raw magneto coil will result in severe ripple and potential driver failure unless the driver explicitly supports AC input or has a robust rectification stage inside.

Most modern LED drivers contain a bridge rectifier, but you must verify the input specification. If the driver expects DC, you should consider adding a simple rectifier circuit if one isn't already present. A standard diode bridge can handle this easily:

```text
Magneto Coil (+) ----|>|----+-------------------[Driver Input +]
                        |    \
                        |     >---> [Optional Capacitor Filter]
                        |    /
Magneto Coil (-) ----|<|----+-------------------[Driver Input -]
```

Place a small capacitor (e.g., 100ÂµF to 470ÂµF) across the input of your LED driver. This smooths out the high-frequency ripple caused by the magneto's intermittent generation profile, preventing the driver from seeing raw spikes that could cause it to reset or overheat.

### Feasibility and Alternatives

Regarding the snowblower engines you mentioned, specifically the Briggs & Stratton 1650 series: many modern variants do indeed come with an integrated alternator (stator) in addition to the ignition magneto. If your unit lacks this feature, it is likely a model variant omission rather than a missing part that can be easily retrofitted into the flywheel housing without machining. Retrofitting a dedicated alternator to a small engine is generally not recommended due to space constraints and cooling issues, but swapping the entire engine for one equipped with an output stator is often the most reliable path forward if you need guaranteed 12V DC power.

For the hovercraft application, if the magneto can spin at sufficient RPMs to maintain voltage above the LED driver's threshold without causing the engine to bog down, it is a viable solution. However, remember that this power source disappears instantly when the engine stops. There is no residual charge stored in the system. If your headlight needs to stay on briefly after shutdown (e.g., for visibility while dismounting), a small 12V capacitor bank or a lightweight lithium-polymer battery in parallel with the magneto output would be required, though this contradicts your goal of "no battery."

Ultimately, the decision hinges on whether the engine's mechanical efficiency will degrade noticeably when lighting the headlight. If the hovercraft slows down perceptibly or struggles to maintain lift at idle due to the electrical load, the magneto is not a sustainable power source for that accessory. In that case, adding a small auxiliary alternator driven by an idler pulley or upgrading the engine to a model with built-in charging capabilities becomes the necessary engineering choice.
